# SK0240 — The control flow does nothing

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A jump, a `default:` section, a `case` label, a `catch` or a `finally` that transfers control to where control was already going.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Cleanup |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `RedundantJumpStatement` (`resharper_redundant_jump_statement_highlighting`) |
| Supersedes | RedundantEmptySwitchSection, RedundantCatchClause, RedundantEmptyFinallyBlock, RedundantCaseLabel, RedundantEnumCaseLabelForDefaultSection |

## Why

⚠ **`catch (X) { throw; }` is the member that matters and the rest are housekeeping beside it.** A rethrowing catch reads as error handling: it is where a reader goes looking for the recovery, the wrapping, the logging — and there is none. `throw;` preserves the stack trace, so unlike `SK2015`'s `throw ex;` there is not even a defect underneath it; the clause is inert, and every question it raises has the answer "nothing happens here", which is what the code would say with no `catch` at all. An empty `finally` is its mirror image and says something stronger still — *this runs whatever happens* — about a block that does nothing. The other three shapes are the same sentence about ordinary control flow: a `continue;` at the end of a loop body jumps to the next iteration that was one statement away, a `return;` at the end of a void body leaves a method that was about to end, a `default:` section that only breaks describes what a `switch` with no matching section already does, and a `case` label sharing its section with `default:` names a value that reaches the same statements without it.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
try {
    Write(path, payload);
} catch (IOException) {
    throw;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
Write(path, payload);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Only the last `catch` of a `try` is ever reported, and that is correctness rather than caution.** Deleting an earlier one changes which handler an exception reaches: in `try { … } catch (IOException) { throw; } catch (Exception e) { Log(e); }` the first clause is what stops an `IOException` being logged, so removing it is a behaviour change wearing a redundancy's clothes. Removing the *last* clause can only leave the exception propagating, which is what the rethrow already did. A `catch` carrying a `when` filter is never reported: the filter runs code, and a filter that returns false leaves the exception to a later clause. ⚠ **Where the reported clause is the only one, the fix has to replace the whole `try` by its block's contents** — `try { … }` alone is CS1524 — and that is offered only when the block declares nothing, because unwrapping a scope moves every local, local function and label it holds into the enclosing scope where a name that was never in conflict can now collide. A try block that declares a local is left alone rather than fixed badly, and so the finding is withheld. The same is true when the `try` is an embedded statement rather than a statement in a block, because the splice would have more than one statement and nowhere to put it. ⚠ **At most one finding per `try` per pass, and that is not tidiness.** A `try { … } catch (X) { throw; } finally { }` matches both the rethrowing-catch shape and the empty-`finally` shape; the two edits are separate spans, so nothing stops `skala fix` applying both — and applying both leaves `try { … }`, which is CS1524. The `catch` is reported and the next pass over the fixed text finds the `finally`, which is a convergent sequence rather than a loop. ⚠ **`goto default;` anywhere in the switch withdraws the `default:` finding** and any `goto case` anywhere in it withdraws every `case`-label finding in it, because the label is the jump's target and deleting it turns a redundancy into CS0159. The `goto case` guard is deliberately coarser than it could be: matching the jump's expression to the label's would mean comparing two constant expressions without a semantic model — `goto case Colour.Red;` against `case Red:` — and being wrong there produces a fix that does not compile. A `case` label is reported only where its section also carries `default:`, which is the only arrangement in which the label selects nothing; a section of `case 1: case 2:` with no `default:` is not this shape, because without `case 2:` the value 2 falls off the end of the switch instead. ⚠ **The `return;` half reads the written return type and never a symbol**, so it matches the `void` keyword, constructors, destructors and `set`/`init`/`add`/`remove` accessors. `async Task` is the same redundancy and is deliberately not matched: `Task` is a name that can be aliased, and answering it needs a semantic model this rule does not ask for. ⚠ **There is no iterator guard, and the belief that one was needed is refuted.** A bare `return;` inside an iterator is not legal C# and does not mean `yield break`: the compiler rejects it with CS1622. The guard was written, committed with a negative fixture, and the fixture failed to compile — an iterator cannot contain the shape this rule matches, so nothing has to exclude it. ⚠ **A comment withdraws the finding only when the fix would delete it, and the first version of this rule got that wrong in two of its shapes.** The guard asked `DescendantTrivia` of the `catch` clause and of the `default:` section — and a node's descendant trivia begins with its first token's *leading* trivia, which is the comment on the line above it. The fix deletes spans that start at the `catch` and `default` keywords, so that comment was never at risk; the guard was withdrawing correct findings to protect text the fix does not touch. Measured rather than reasoned about: a `//` above the `catch` took the count from 1 to 0, and the same above `default:` did too. The guards now ask about the span the fix deletes. ⚠ The unwrap case is the exception and keeps a wider guard, because it replaces the whole `try` by its block's contents: what it discards is the header up to `{` and the tail from `}` onwards, so a comment written between `}` and `catch` *is* deleted by that fix and does withdraw the finding. A preprocessor directive in the clause's own trivia withdraws every shape whatever the span, because a directive is a region rather than content. ⚠ The boolean-expression members of this family — `RedundantBoolCompare`, `DoubleNegationOperator`, `NegativeEqualityExpression`, `RedundantTernaryExpression`, `RedundantLogicalConditionalExpressionOperand` — are **not** covered. Each needs to know an operand's type before it is redundant rather than meaningful (`x == true` is not redundant for a `bool?`, and `!` may be overloaded), which would make this rule semantic and stop it running on a loose file. `RedundantIfElseBlock` and `RedundantSwitchExpressionArms` are not covered either: the first unwraps a scope on a control-flow judgement about the *then* branch, and the second needs to know which arms a switch expression's input type can still reach.
